lessons.title: Understanding and tracking costs
lessons.html:
Understanding and tracking costs

In poultry production, margins are small and volumes are large. A manager who tracks costs per flock and per unit of output, and acts on deviations, protects the profitability of the unit.

Cost centres

Allocate costs to cost centres - each house or flock, the egg room, the hatchery, maintenance - so that performance can be compared. Main cost categories:

  • Feed (by phase and delivery).
  • Chicks or pullets.
  • Labour (including overtime and casual labour).
  • Energy: electricity, gas, coal, generator diesel.
  • Health: vaccines, medication, disinfectants, vet fees.
  • Litter, packaging, egg trays and cartons.
  • Repairs, maintenance and spares.
  • Overheads allocated by an agreed basis.

Unit cost measures

MeasureCalculation
Cost per bird placedTotal flock cost / birds placed
Cost per kg live weightTotal flock cost / total kg sold
Feed cost per kg live weightFCR x feed price per kg
Cost per dozen eggsTotal layer cost for period / dozens produced
Feed per dozen eggskg feed / dozens produced

Example

If a flock's FCR is 1.6 and feed costs R8 per kg, feed cost is R12.80 per kg live weight. If FCR improves to 1.55 at the same price, feed cost falls to R12.40 per kg - a saving of 40 cents on every kilogram produced. Across a large flock this is a significant amount.

Budget versus actual

Compare actual costs with the budget each month and at the end of every flock. Calculate variances (actual minus budget) and investigate significant ones. Separate price variances (feed cost more per tonne) from usage variances (more feed used per bird) because they have different causes and solutions.

lessons.title: Stock control systems
lessons.html:
Stock control systems

What stock is held

  • Feed in silos and bags.
  • Live birds - the most valuable stock on the farm.
  • Eggs in the egg room and cold store.
  • Vaccines and medicines, often cold-chain items with expiry dates.
  • Disinfectants, detergents and pest control products.
  • Litter, packaging and egg trays.
  • Fuel and spares.

Receiving stock

  1. Check delivery against the order: product, quantity, batch, expiry.
  2. Inspect quality: feed form and smell, damaged packaging, vaccine temperature on arrival.
  3. Weigh bulk feed deliveries or confirm with weighbridge slips.
  4. Record in the stock register or system and file delivery notes.
  5. Report discrepancies to the supplier immediately.

Storage

Store feed dry, off the floor, protected from rodents and birds. Store vaccines in monitored fridges with daily temperature records. Store chemicals in locked, ventilated stores, separated by type, as labels and Act 36 of 1947 require. Use first-expiry, first-out rotation.

Issuing stock

Issue against a request or job, recording item, quantity, house or cost centre, date and person. This links consumption to cost centres and allows tracking.

Stock counts and reconciliation

Do regular physical counts and reconcile with records:

Opening stock + receipts - issues = expected closing stock. Compare with the physical count. Investigate differences: recording errors, wastage, spoilage or theft.

Bird reconciliation

For each flock: birds placed - mortality - culls - birds sold = birds remaining. At depletion, birds caught must reconcile with birds placed minus recorded deaths. Unexplained losses must be investigated.

Feed reconciliation

Feed delivered minus feed remaining in silos should equal feed consumed. Compare consumption with the standard intake for the bird numbers and age. High apparent consumption may mean wastage, spillage, rodents, recording errors or theft.

lessons.title: Controlling costs and reporting
lessons.html:
Controlling costs and reporting

Cost control actions

AreaActions
FeedCorrect feeder heights and levels to cut wastage; repair spills; control rodents; match feed phases to age; monitor FCR
MortalityBrooding quality, biosecurity, early problem detection
EnergyInsulation, maintained heaters and fans, correct controller settings, LED lighting, generator efficiency
LabourEfficient rosters, controlled overtime, trained staff
HealthCorrect vaccine handling to avoid wastage; treatment only on diagnosis
EggsReduce cracks and dirty eggs through equipment maintenance and frequent collection
StockPrevent expiry, spoilage and theft

Ordering

Set minimum stock levels and reorder points for key items, considering usage rates and supplier lead times. Avoid overstocking perishable items such as vaccines; avoid running out of critical items such as feed, generator fuel or disinfectant. Compare supplier quotes for major items and negotiate.

Preventing losses

  • Control access to stores and keys.
  • Separate duties where possible: the person who receives stock is not the only one who counts it.
  • Do surprise counts.
  • Investigate all significant variances and document outcomes.

Reporting

Prepare monthly and end-of-flock reports for management:

  1. Production results: birds, weights, mortality, FCR or egg production.
  2. Costs by category and per unit against budget, with variance explanations.
  3. Stock on hand, reconciliation results and losses.
  4. Actions taken and recommendations.

Present clear tables and highlight the few items that matter most. Recommend specific actions with estimated savings.

Key points

  • Allocate costs to cost centres and track unit costs.
  • Separate price and usage variances when comparing with budget.
  • Receive, store and issue stock with records and checks.
  • Reconcile feed, birds and other stock regularly and investigate differences.
  • Set reorder points and report costs and stock with clear recommendations.
